newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Key facts about elections in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Key facts about elections in Chechnya.

text.p: Voters in Chechnya, which fought a bitter war to try to break away from Russia, are electing a regional president and a local parliament on Monday.
Thirteen candidates are vying for a five-year presidential term in the southern, mainly Moslem region, which formally remains part of Russia. Three other candidates dropped out before voting began.
To win in the first round, candidates need to win more than half the votes cast (50 percent plus one vote).
If no candidate achieves this, a runoff round will be held two weeks later between the two candidates with most votes.
If fewer than 50 percent of voters registered on electoral rolls take part in either the first or second rounds, then that round is declared invalid and is repeated within one month.
The Central Election Commission says about 850 candidates are seeking election to the 63-member parliament, which will also serve for five years.
All seats are allocated on the basis of single-member constituencies, although candidates may list party affiliation.

Under the constitution the president appoints ministers, who must be approved by a majority in parliament. But he or she has power to disband the body, as the late president Dzhokhar Dudayev did in 1993.
Voters may cast ballots in 423 regular polling places from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. (0400 to 1700 GMT).
Preliminary results are expected to start coming late on Monday or early on Tuesday and final results must be certified and published within five days of the end of voting.

The Central Election Commission puts the registered electorate at about 400,000, but the figure does not include refugees who will vote in special stations or persons who returned to the republic recently.
More than a dozen polling places were set up near Chechnya's borders with the neighbouring Russian republics of Ingushetia and Dagestan, as well as the Stavropol region, to allow refugees to vote.
The Central Election Commission said it expected between 50,000 and 60,000 refugees to cast ballots in these stations.
